branch-detail called journal/turns, which SELECTs every turn of the whole run with every column, then filtered for one branch in Clojure. So every branch click paid a 5.8MB whole-run fetch (gen-14) regardless of branch size, with 5.5MB of it assistant_text that no display path reads. Measured on the live server: 6-turn branches 2.6-4.5s, a 51-turn branch >50s. The GUI's socket timeout is 45s, so large branches never loaded.

Worse, the client discarded the failure: refresh-branch-log! only swapped state on (:ok r), so a timeout left :branch-log nil and the panel read '(loading full turn results and encodings...)' forever, with no way to tell a slow fetch from a dead one. The poll loop then refired it on every event touching the branch, queueing a fresh doomed 45s request about once a second. Same shape as the crashed-run-still-marked-running bug.

Also fixed alongside: the poll loop compared the selected NODE id against event branch_ids, but an artifact node's id is '<branch>@<turn>', so artifact panels never refreshed at all.
acceptance_criteria: A branch with 50+ turns loads its panel, and a failed fetch says so instead of showing a permanent loading line.
close_reason: journal/branch-turns filters by branch in SQL (using the idx_turns_run index, which was going unused) and drops assistant_text/reasoning_text from the projection — 5,857,814 bytes to 69,366, an 84x reduction. journal/turns keeps its full-row shape because resume replays assistant_text from it. Client side: refresh-branch-log! now records the failure in :branch-log-error and the panel says why it is missing, noting the live activity and attempts above it are complete; and the poll loop compares against selected-branch-id so artifact panels refresh too. Tests: branch-turns-reads-one-branch-and-leaves-the-bulk-behind.

title: Judge verdicts are unattributable — reasoning is never journalled
description:
A faithfulness rejection leaves claim-status = unfaithful and nothing else. The judge's answer, the gap it named and its reasoning are all discarded, so there is no way to tell a caught defect from a misfire.

Hit for real on gen-14 turn 10: a#350 (octave, mod-105 slack enumeration for {3,5,7,11}) was rejected as unfaithful. Its arithmetic is independently confirmed correct — all eight scaled constants and the minimum -647 at (1,1,2,4) reproduce exactly — so either the reviewer caught a framing defect (the claim names four residues but the encoding also fixes a3=a5=a7=0 by translation symmetry, undisclosed) or it misfired on the abandoned glpk scratch block the workspace log now carries. The journal cannot distinguish them.

This blocks the question that decides whether the whole faithfulness gate is worth having: what is its false-positive rate on real work.

Also note: only rejections being visible would bias the answer, so passes must be recorded too, and a transport failure that fails closed must be distinguishable from a rejection on the merits.
acceptance_criteria: Every judge call records its label, verdict, named gaps and reasoning in the journal, for passes and failures alike.
close_reason:
Fixed in 8de8632: note-verdict! inside judge/2 records label, verdict, named gaps, prompt size and the answer (reasoning stripped, capped at 4000 chars) for every judge call — faithfulness, review and audit alike, passes as well as failures, with transport failures distinguishable from rejections on the merits. Tests: a-judge-verdict-is-journalled-with-its-reasoning, a-judge-verdict-that-passes-is-journalled-too.

The motivating question is now answered, offline, by reconstructing the prompt: the judge was RIGHT both times. Its gap on a#350 — 'the claim is for support {3,5,7,11}, but the artifact never uses the prime 11' — is correct, since 11 is coprime to 105 and enters the argument only through the eight scaled constants, which neither artifact derives. Not deployed: needs a jolt serve restart, which would end gen-14.

title: Faithfulness checks don't cover lean, octave, template, or refutations
description:
After a701e51, verify_smt and verify (prolog) run deterministic structural checks then the LLM judge. Still uncovered:

1. verify_lean, verify_octave, verify_template have neither layer. gen-13 a#344 is a confirmed artifact whose entire evidence is a glpk floating-point value (1.014488 > 1, self-declared tolerance 0.001) with nothing comparing computation to claim. Its conclusion happened to be correct and separately proved exactly, so nothing rested on it — but a numeric artifact with a hand-stated tolerance was recorded as engine-confirmed unexamined.

2. REFUTATIONS skip both layers, since the checks run only on would-be confirmations. gen-13 a#336 recorded a refutation whose claim asserted unrestricted domains while its encoding pinned y0 = 0. A refuted artifact asserts the negation, which is still a fact entering the run's record and readable by other branches.

3. Known limitation of the count check, pinned by test: a claim stating FEWER constraints than the encoding asserts is undetectable, because a surplus is what correct artifacts look like (bounds, symmetry breaks). gen-12's a#321/a#324 said '14 inequalities' over 15. Catching that needs identifying which asserts are class constraints, or a claim-internal consistency check (the claim listed three families of 3, 5 and 7).

Suggested order: extend the structural+judge pair to octave first (numeric claims are the least self-evidencing), then refutations, then lean/template.
acceptance_criteria: A confirmed octave/lean/template artifact and a refutation both face the same checks verify_smt does.
close_reason: Octave, Lean and verify_template now run structural checks then the judge, and refutations face both layers. New deterministic checks: octave expressions that compute nothing (a#344), unsat over an undisclosed partial family pin (a#336), and claims whose enumerated index families exceed their stated total (a#321/a#324, the case the assert count could not reach). Validated against all 348 artifacts in the journal: 1 of 42 octave rows objected to, 1 of 108 smt rows, 2 of 348 claims — every one a known-bad artifact, zero false positives. Also fixed: a Lean snippet the REPL rejects no longer records a :refuted artifact, and verify_template no longer claims its cross-check makes review unnecessary.

title: Faithfulness check can be satisfied by weakening the claim, not fixing the encoding
description:
The vf-slr faithfulness judge compares claim to encoding and passes when they agree. Agreement can be reached from either end, and restating the claim is far cheaper than fixing the formula — so the check creates an incentive to drift the claim down onto whatever was encoded.

Observed live in gen-12 (run 98d0423e), branch B2, within four turns:

  a#318  p=5 base 662, 135 wrongly counted coprime to 5, no assignable 135 term  -> PASSED (miss)
  a#319  base corrected to 655, 135 still absent                                 -> blocked (correct)
  a#320  regressed to 662                                                        -> blocked (correct)
  a#321  same defective encoding as a#320, CLAIM REWRITTEN to transcribe it      -> CONFIRMED

a#321's claim now reads 'there is no assignment ... such that ALL of the following 14 inequalities hold: ... 662 + sum over m in {5,15,35,45,105,315,945} ...'. It spells out the wrong base and the omitted modulus as the content of the claim. The encoding is genuinely faithful to that claim and Z3's unsat genuinely establishes it, so the judge was right to pass it. The artifact is true and establishes nothing about covering systems.

Two things to fix:

1. tools.clj run-tool verify_smt result text for :unfaithful literally instructs this: 'or restate the claim to match what you encoded'. Drop that half of the sentence.

2. The check needs a relevance leg, not just a consistency leg. Candidates: judge the claim against the branch's pinned thesis rather than only against the encoding; or reject claims that are transcriptions of their own formula (a claim naming explicit coefficient lists is describing an artifact, not a theorem).

Also worth a cheap deterministic pre-check that needs no LLM: for any claim naming a layered condition mod p, verify the coprime base equals sum of L/m over {m in support : p does not divide m}, and that every m with p|m appears as an assignable term. That arithmetic would have caught a#318, a#319, a#320 and a#321 without a model call.
acceptance_criteria: A branch cannot get a confirmation by restating the claim to match a defective encoding; the misleading half of the :unfaithful message is gone.
close_reason: Fixed across 965b459 and a701e51. The 'or restate the claim to match what you encoded' escape is gone from the :unfaithful message. More importantly the drift incentive is largely removed: the deterministic checks in agent.faithful cannot be argued with, so rewriting the claim no longer buys a confirmation past a bad coefficient or a missing constraint. Known limitation, pinned by test: a claim stating FEWER constraints than the encoding asserts (gen-12's 14-vs-15) is not detectable, since a surplus of asserts is what correct artifacts look like.

title: A shipped branch is never closed in the run record
description:
tools/done sets :status :done and :final-answer. Both DB-close paths in beam/run-loop miss that combination: the post-cull loop writes only branches with (not (:final-answer b)), and the run-end done-branch loop writes only (state/active? b) ones. So a branch that ships keeps status='active' in the branches table forever and never emits a branch-closed event.

Seen in gen-10 (05ecb88a): the run completed with all nine surviving branches shipped, and all nine still read 'active'. The GUI folds status from branch-closed events, so a finished run renders nine live branches, and the working indicator keys on :active too. Their engines are also held to run end instead of being disposed when the branch stops working.
close_reason: Closed

title: Erdos-Selfridge odd covering campaign: run generations 6-9
description:
STANDING INSTRUCTION (user, 2026-08-07): keep running seeded generations of the odd-covering campaign for at least 3-4 more rounds after gen-5, unless the $2000 problem is solved first.

Each round: wait for the current run to finish, verify its numbers by hand, update docs/odd-covering.md (frontier table + proofs), then launch the next generation with seed_run pointing at the run just finished, an ambition floor naming already-settled sets as unshippable, and targets chosen in Pareto-minimal order (maximize density slack, minimize lcm, minimize modulus count).

Run ids so far: c45ac428 (gen1), b84d2263 (gen2), 61de2075 (gen3), c5dcc35f (gen4), 7f4af6b7 (gen5, in flight).

STOP EARLY if: an actual odd distinct covering system is found and verified (then the work is verification and write-up, not another generation), or a generation returns nothing new AND leaves no usable direction - report that rather than burning another run.

The structural thread worth pushing: the entangled uncovered fraction is decaying slowly (17/45=0.378, 80/225=0.356, 47/135=0.348, 221/675=0.327). Does it decay to zero or hit a positive floor? A family-wide engine-confirmed lower bound would rule out odd coverings for infinitely many modulus sets at once - the strongest result this campaign could produce.
notes: gen8 74abc803 aborted at turn 184 (22 confirmed, journaled and seeded forward) to deploy the evolutionary loop. gen9 94452de2 is the first run with it: branch-out gate (reproduction on confirmation), crossover-block (children open holding every other lineage's confirmed results), stop-on-first-done? off (a ship no longer ends the run). Started at beam width 2 so growth has to be earned.
close_reason: gens 6-9 complete. gen9 produced the campaign's strongest result: a {3,5,7}-supported density-feasible set proved non-covering by a Lean-checked partition argument on a search space of 1.7e9 assignments. Evolutionary loop shipped and validated live (forked: 2).

title: Exhaustion progress report (never ship nothing)
description: UCLA Track B: when nothing ships, emit an honest structured progress report instead of a failure string - never ship nothing, never ship a lie. Extends the planned residual-objectives item: on beam exhaustion assemble per-branch undischarged thesis sub-claims, best confirmed artifacts with provenance, top shared-failure-log entries, and gate history summary, explicitly labeled not-a-solution. Do-not-claim-more-than-proved is mechanical for us: only engine-confirmed artifacts appear as established.
acceptance_criteria: Exhausted runs return structured report in message content + harness field: confirmed artifacts w/ provenance, undischarged sub-claims, relevant failures, labeled as progress report. No unconfirmed claim rendered as established (test). Bare beam-exhausted string gone.
close_reason: report assembly + rendering + API wiring + honesty tests; 100 tests green

title: Wind-down arbiter rung at late turn budget
description: UCLA reserves a deadline tail exclusively for assembly and shipping. Our 85% turn-budget notice informs but does not steer. Add an arbiter rung: at the late notice, the steer becomes assemble-and-ship-what-you-have (today only a human intervention example). Declares a prediction like other gates (branch calls audit or review within N turns) settled from the journal; sits below human directives and done-block in priority; one-shot re-fire guard.
acceptance_criteria: New gate in gates.edn with kind + doc. Arbiter rung with priority slot, prediction, re-fire guard. Prompt file for the steer. Test: scripted branch nearing cap receives exactly one wind-down steer, prediction settles; probe stays silent on a branch that ships early.
close_reason: wind-down gate, prompt, predictions, tests; 99 tests green

title: Audit restatement and is-relaxation axis
description: Audit must restate, self-contained, what the answer actually establishes (no anaphora), plus an is-relaxation flag comparing that against the pinned thesis - a failed attempt at the full claim is NOT a relaxation. Unlike UCLA we never re-pin the claim to the restatement (their ratchet let proofs pass against shrunken claims); drift is recorded against the original thesis. Claim-evidence gate extended: an artifact confirming only a weakened claim cannot substantiate the full answer, generalizing the existential bucket.
acceptance_criteria: Audit output schema carries restatement + is-relaxation. Anti-conflation rule in prompt. Thesis stays pinned; drift journaled. Claim-evidence gate refuses relaxation-only coverage; scripted transcript proves it. Existential-bucket tests still pass.
close_reason: ESTABLISHED/RELAXATION parsing, thesis-drift journal, done-gate relaxation refusal; 98 tests green

title: Named exemption lists in audit/review prompts
description: UCLA strictness was usable only because routine facts are exempted by name with DO-NOT-FLAG lists; without them the referee drowns everything in nitpicks and burns the done-block budget on non-gaps. Add named exemption lists to our audit/review prompt files (routine algebraic steps, standard library lemmas already engine-confirmed, phrasing/exposition items). Measure by max-done-blocks firings before/after on the probe set; the false-positive probe must still refuse.
acceptance_criteria: Exemption lists in prompt files as data-like sections. Probe set unchanged results for real gaps (false-positive probe still refuses; claim-evidence transcript still blocks). Bench note comparing done-block firings.
close_reason: exemption list wired to both judges + digest; 93 tests green

title: Judge-not-vote contract for verdict aggregation
description: Encode the UCLA consensus judge principle as a mechanical contract wherever more than one verdict about the same claim exists: LLM verdicts are evidence, never votes - no code path may majority-count them. Counting is legitimate only for independent engine confirmations (Prolog/Z3/Lean agreeing), which compose empirically. If multiple review/audit verdicts are ever aggregated, aggregation goes through a single judge that must record per-disagreement reasoning in the journal. Ship the contract and tests now so any future multi-model review lands inside it.
acceptance_criteria: A verdict-aggregation namespace with the contract in its docstring. Tests: aggregating N LLM verdicts by count throws or is unrepresentable; engine-confirmation counting allowed; judge path records reasoning per disagreement. Gate table untouched.

title: Patch-existence severity criterion in audit/review

title: Q-1 for arbitrary instances needs a scaling subroutine, not arc subdivision
description:
Arc subdivision builds on the order of S unit arcs per edge. For grid instances S <= 2V so this is polynomial, but Q-1 says ARBITRARY instance, where b is written in binary and S can be exponential in the encoding size.

The coefficients are not the obstacle: with D = S, H is on the order of E*S^2, so log H is O(log E + log S). What is needed is a separable convex integer min-cost flow subroutine polynomial in log S — proximity or capacity scaling. gen-24 a#847/a#848 are a branch working this.

Either deliver that, or prove hardness, or state precisely that the result is restricted to instance classes with polynomially bounded S.

title: Prove the stage-2 box bound |k_e| <= S directly, not through a grid-specific reindexing
description:
gen-22's remaining gap (a) is the existence of a bound on stage-2-optimal flows. B3 is closing it by proving an alternating-snake bijection between an MxN grid and a path, then pulling the verified path-flow construction back through it. That works only on rectangular grids and needs the Hamiltonian path as a lemma.

The general argument is shorter and covers any graph. If k is C-minimal and Q-minimal among C-minimal flows, its sign-oriented support has no directed cycle: subtracting a unit around one preserves divergence, weakly decreases C, and strictly decreases Q. An acyclic flow with divergence b decomposes into paths carrying S = sum of positive divergences in total, so |k_e| <= S on every edge.

Checked independently on 3,215 random instances with zero weights present: no stage-2 optimum violates it, and the bound is attained on 2,035 of them, so it is tight. Note S, not E*S -- a#702's bound is weaker than necessary.

This is a note about the shape of the argument, for whichever run picks the gap up. Not a harness change.
notes: Half done. gen-24's a#774 proves the general form with no grid anywhere: given any acyclic relation containing the support, every supported edge satisfies f e <= S. The grid-specific snake route is abandoned as this issue asked. What remains is only the acyclicity hypothesis itself — gen-25 TARGET 1 — so this issue now duplicates that and should close when (A) lands.

title: A tool to fetch an artifact's encoding by id
description:
The ledger (vf-ckq) lists claims with ids and leaves the encodings out, so the code costs a turn only when a branch actually wants it rather than riding in every context block. That only works if an id is actionable.

No tool currently returns an artifact by id. The shared block inlines a truncated encoding (vf-8wp, capped at 700 chars) precisely because there was no way to ask for one; with a fetch tool that cap can stay small and the full encoding stays available.

Should return the claim, kind, tier, verdict, claim_status and full code — including for REFUTED artifacts, where the encoding is the thing that shows why the line is closed and is what stops a sibling re-attempting it.
design:
Read-only, no verification, no artifact produced — it is a lookup, so it must be :neutral rather than :success, or it would reset the failure counter and read as progress. Scope to the current run: cross-run reach would let a branch cite something the run never established, which the done gate's evidence rungs are built to prevent.

Name it for what it does to a ledger id rather than after the table.
acceptance_criteria: A branch can turn a ledger id into the full encoding in one call, and doing so neither counts as progress nor clears its failure count.
close_reason:
Built as one mechanism instead of three. journal/ledger reads the artifacts table — which already has claim_status where shared_artifacts does not — so refutations become visible with no migration and no second sharing path; that is vf-0tk solved via the ledger rather than by widening shareable?, which I had filed. Complete rather than FTS-sampled, since the value is that a branch can trust the absence of a line. Two sections so a refutation cannot read as a confirmation. fetch_artifact makes the ids actionable, :neutral so a lookup cannot clear a failure count, run-scoped, and works on refuted artifacts where the encoding is what shows why the line is closed.

THE PART THAT NEARLY WENT WRONG: the block is appended every turn, so a naive wiring accumulates one copy per turn — gen-17's ledger over an 80-turn branch would have been 854,800 chars / 211k tokens, four times the largest context ever recorded. message/strip-stale-ledgers drops all but the newest on the way to the wire, following the strip-think-blocks precedent; the branch keeps every copy so the journal and resume stay faithful. 80 turns now costs 10,642 chars instead of 854,800. Claims capped at 180 chars with the full statement one fetch away: gen-18's ledger 6,795 -> 3,805 tokens, gen-20's 428.

264 tests, 1324 assertions, 0 failures.

title: Lean and Octave session handles live only in the branch map, so error paths lose them
description:
Observed live during gen-20, 2026-08-13. PID 22821, /tools/lean-repl/.lake/build/bin/repl, ppid 1, elapsed 1h55m, RSS ~4.8GB. Its lake parent is gone and it was reparented to init.

Lean sessions are spawned as 'lake env <repl>', so lake is the child and repl the grandchild. When lake dies without taking repl with it, repl survives — destroy-tree is a shutdown hook rather than a guarantee, which is already noted in the FD_CLOEXEC work (vf-k0a).

DIAGNOSIS, from lsof pipe endpoints. The session is HALF connected, which is why nothing reclaims it:
  - the server still holds the read ends of the orphan's stdout and stderr (orphan fd 1 peer and fd 2 peer both match server devices);
  - the write end of the orphan's stdin is NOT held by the server, so the server cannot send it a command.
So it is unreachable for work but still wired for reads. Nothing notices it is dead, and it holds its Mathlib heap indefinitely. Seven Lean REPLs were alive at the time; one was this.

NOT killed, deliberately: gen-20 was mid-flight and the server still holds pipe read ends, so killing it could disturb a live session. It is ~5GB on a box at 81% free, which is not urgent. Clean up after the run and confirm the pattern then.
design:
ROOT CAUSE IS IN JOLT, NOT HERE. Filed as jolt-hpdu.

jolt's host/chez/java/process.ss:723 hardcodes ProcessHandle.descendants to an empty vector, and babashka.process's destroy-tree (vendor/process/src/babashka/process.cljc:165) is implemented as destroy over (cons handle descendants). Empty descendants means destroy-tree IS destroy. veriframe spawns 'lake env <repl>', so destroy-tree kills lake and the repl grandchild survives.

veriframe is calling the right API with the right intent — engine/lean_repl.clj:69 passes :shutdown p/destroy-tree and dispose calls it directly. Nothing here is wrong. The fix belongs in jolt.

WHAT IS STILL WORTH DOING HERE, independently of the jolt fix: a session whose process is unreachable should be reaped rather than left registered. The observed orphan was half-connected — the server still held the read ends of its stdout and stderr but not the write end of its stdin — so it could never be driven again while still looking alive. That is a detectable state and belongs to whoever owns session lifecycle, which is this repo. Belt and braces: even with destroy-tree fixed, a repl can die on its own.
acceptance_criteria: A Lean REPL whose parent died is reaped rather than surviving the run, and the leak rate per run is measured.
notes: RE-DIAGNOSED 2026-08-15: the jolt-hpdu premise is WRONG. destroy-tree reaches the grandchild — verified twice, on a plain sh grandchild and on the exact lake env repl spawn; both times descendants returned the child and both processes died. So the 19 leaked repls were never disposed at all, rather than disposed unsuccessfully. This is a veriframe bug, not a jolt one, and it is not blocked on anything. See docs/jolt-bugs.md. The descendant-collecting teardown we added is defensive and harmless but was not the fix; the real question is which code path drops a session handle without calling dispose!.
close_reason: Fixed and empirically verified. gen-27 started at 05:16 UTC, after the session registry landed at 05:02, created sessions, completed, and left none behind — every live repl belongs to gen-28, and the sole survivor predates the registry. Root cause was not jolt's destroy-tree (see docs/jolt-bugs.md) but session handles living only in the branch map, which three error paths discard.

title: Seeded artifacts crowd in-run ones out of the shared-artifact block
description:
gen-20 was seeded from gen-19 (16 artifacts). Of the 91 shared-artifact-hit events it has produced, 67 served SEEDED artifacts and only 24 served artifacts the run itself confirmed:

  seed:B2.2  33      B3     10
  seed:B4    18      B4.2    5
  seed:B2    15      B1      5
  seed:B3     1      B4      4

The seeded ones are gen-19's dipole-square and stage-2-classification results — which gen-20's problem statement already states in full, in a section headed 'Settled by previous runs, do NOT spend turns reproving any of it'. So roughly three quarters of the sharing budget is spent re-telling the branch something its own system prompt already carries, while the in-run lemmas that branches are actively duplicating (vf-*) get the remainder.

The ranking in loop/context-block treats seeded and in-run artifacts identically — both come back from artifacts/similar or artifacts/recent with no notion of provenance — and a completed run contributes a full pool at turn 0 while the live run's pool starts empty. So seeds win on volume from the start.
design: Options: rank in-run artifacts above seeded ones; cap the seeded share of the block; or drop seeded artifacts from the block entirely on the grounds that seeding already injects them into the problem statement, which would make the block purely a cross-branch channel and match what it is documented to be ('Confirmed by other branches'). The last is the simplest and most honest — the block's own header is currently inaccurate for two thirds of what it serves.
acceptance_criteria: The shared block is dominated by artifacts the run produced, and seeded material is not re-served alongside a prompt that already states it.
notes: Cross-ref: the in-run lemmas being crowded out are the duplicated scalarization proofs in vf-8wp. The two issues compound — seeds take three quarters of the slots, and what does get through is unusable for reuse anyway.

Both fixed, TDD, 257 tests / 1276 assertions / 0 failures.

The code was already selected by similar/recent and copied by seed-from-run! for exactly this purpose; only the renderer dropped it. Block also now says 'Cite these by name and re-verify in one call; do not re-derive them.'

vf-yxs: fixed in two places, because ranking alone was not enough. artifacts/prefer-in-run puts in-run entries before seeded ones preserving relevance order within each group, AND context-block now fetches 3x what it displays before ranking down — reordering a top-5 that is already all seeds just reorders seeds, which is the normal early case since a completed run contributes its whole pool at turn 0.

CORRECTION to my filed design: I had proposed dropping seeded artifacts from the block entirely, on the grounds that seeding already injects them into the problem statement. That was wrong. Seeding does not touch the problem statement — gen-20's statement restated gen-19's results because I wrote it that way by hand. A campaign that seeds without restating would have lost them. Ranked, not filtered.

title: Shared artifacts show the claim but not the proof, so siblings re-derive instead of reusing
description:
Three branches in gen-20 independently proved the same scalarization lemma: B4 turn 8 (Hf/Hg), B3 turn 19 (H/K), B4.2 turn 20 (alpha/beta). Same result, renamed variables, three slow-tier Lean proofs. That is 3 of the run's first 6 confirmed artifacts spent on one lemma.

Sharing was ON — a seeded run forces it (beam.clj:671) — and the branches were SHOWN each other's work: the two scalarization claims were each served 5 times through the shared-artifact block. So this is not a discovery failure. They saw it and re-proved it anyway.

The reason is in store/artifacts.clj:123. The block renders claim text only:

  - [B3 lean/slow] Scalarization yields lexicographic minimizer: with H > K*Qmax + Lrange and K > Lrange, ...

No code, no theorem statement. For a Lean or SMT artifact the CODE is the reusable thing — a branch that wants to build on a sibling's lemma needs the exact statement to reference, and a one-line prose summary is not one. Re-deriving is the only move available to it. The branches behaved rationally; the block is what is underpowered.

Distinct from the done()-evidence path, which does consult journal/corroborating-artifacts so a sibling's claim can cover tokens in a shipped answer. That is about ATTRIBUTION. This is about REUSE, and nothing serves it.
design:
Include the code for confirmed slow-tier artifacts in the block, or give the model a tool to fetch a shared artifact's code by id — the second is probably better, since inlining every proof would blow the block's size budget and the block re-renders every turn.

Watch the interaction with faithfulness: a branch citing a sibling's theorem must not be able to pass it off as its own verification, and the audit already refuses answers whose specifics no artifact covers. Reuse should make the provenance MORE explicit, not less.

title: Compare arms on dispersion and blow-up counts, not just means
description:
Third piece of vf-fq6. The reporting, and the part most easily got wrong.

veriframe's interesting effects are blow-ups stopping, not typical runs improving — branches culled for nothing, gates firing without effect, a run that never touches the slow tier. A comparison gated on the control arm's own spread cannot see those, because the spread is precisely what the change removes: the treatment gets measured against the variance it eliminated and reads as noise.

So report, per arm: the blow-up count (runs that culled a branch for zero artifacts, runs with no slow-tier artifact, runs exceeding some turn multiple), max-min dispersion, and the mean. Let dispersion thresholds be coarser than mean thresholds, since range at small n is a weaker statistic and should claim less. State n on every comparison, and refuse to aggregate across models or scenarios whose directions disagree.
design: Keyed by prompt-digest so a behavioural change is attributable to a prompt or gate revision. Present the counts first and the means last — the ordering matters, because a mean that reads as noise beside a 3-of-6 to 0-of-6 blow-up change invites the wrong conclusion.
acceptance_criteria: Two arms of the cheap scenario can be compared, with blow-up counts and dispersion reported alongside means and n stated.

title: A cheap fixed scenario that can be run repeatedly for arm comparison
description:
Second piece of vf-fq6, and the one that makes the rest affordable.

A campaign generation is hours of provider spend, so comparing arms at that scale is not viable. What is needed is a small problem with a known answer, low max_turns and a narrow beam, that finishes in minutes and still exercises the machinery under test: gates firing, artifacts being verified and refused, branches being culled.

The scenario has to be able to SEE the effects in question. A problem that never provokes a __no_call__ turn cannot measure a prefill; one that never reaches the slow tier cannot measure tier-escalation. Pick or construct it against that requirement rather than for convenience, and say plainly which effects it can and cannot see.
design: Fixed problem text with a known-correct answer so correctness is checkable without a judge. Record prompt-digest with each run so arms are attributable.
acceptance_criteria: The scenario runs in minutes, produces gate firings and at least one cull, and its correctness is checkable mechanically.

title: Capture the provider's cache hit and miss token counts
description:
Smallest piece of vf-fq6, useful on its own.

adapter/openai.clj's parse-chat keeps only prompt-tokens, completion-tokens and total-tokens from the usage object. Providers that do prefix caching return hit and miss counts alongside those, and veriframe discards them.

Without those numbers there is no way to answer whether a wide beam thrashes the prefix cache. Each branch carries its own growing message list, so the beam holds N diverging prefixes at once — whether that is cheap or expensive is currently unknowable, and it bears directly on the cost of running width 5 rather than width 3.
design: TDD. Tests first: a usage object carrying the cache fields yields them; one without them yields the existing three fields and no nils that downstream code has to guard. Journal them with the turn so the question is answerable retrospectively, the way assistant_text made vf-ap8's backtest possible.
acceptance_criteria: Cache hit/miss tokens are captured when the provider sends them, and absent cleanly when it does not.
close_reason: Implemented and tested. Usage capture turned out bigger than filed: the adapter parsed usage and client/chat returned it, but the agent loop dropped it and turns had no columns, so the harness could not report what a run cost at all. Migration v4 adds prompt/completion/total plus the cache split, nullable so a provider-error turn does not claim to be free.

title: Backtest near-duplicate responses across the four completed runs
description:
First step of vf-ap8, and possibly the only one. Costs no provider spend.

turns.assistant_text is journalled for every turn of gen-17 (0d0c3560), gen-18 (65d50333), gen-19 (cd58e618) and gen-20 (36bf3163). Score consecutive responses within each branch for near-duplication and report: how often a near-duplicate precedes a __no_call__ turn, how often one precedes a cull, and what the base rate is on turns that led to neither.

The base rate is the part that decides the issue. Branches legitimately repeat themselves — a branch retrying a Lean proof produces near-identical text on purpose — so a high similarity rate among healthy turns means a naive detector would fire on honest work and the issue closes with a measurement instead of code.
design: A one-off analysis, not shipped code. Report the numbers on the issue. Only if repetition clearly discriminates failing turns from healthy ones does a detector get written.
acceptance_criteria: Measured rates for all four runs recorded on vf-ap8, with an explicit recommendation to build or not build.
close_reason: Measured across 18 runs / 3,464 consecutive turn pairs (far more than the four originally scoped — every run with assistant_text populated). Recommendation: DO NOT build the prose detector. Details on vf-ap8.

title: Prefill the predicted tool name when a gate fires with a prediction
description:
The payoff of vf-tso, and the answer to vf-9sa.

Gates already carry a :prediction naming what the branch is expected to do — 'the branch calls review, audit, or done', 'the branch runs a slow-tier check', 'the branch calls branch_theses'. gen-19 settled those 4 met to 22 unmet, and vf-9sa's finding is that suggestion does not bind where withholding does.

Where a prediction names a specific tool, prefill the fence and that name — ```tool-call\n{\"name\": \"review\" — so the next turn cannot be prose. Predictions that name a disjunction or a behaviour rather than a tool ('changes technique') get the bare fence prefill or nothing.

This is also the cheapest fix for vf-lho: tier-escalation says 'the branch runs a slow-tier check', which is not a callable name, and went 0-for-4. Naming verify_template or proof_start in the prefill makes it callable.
design: Do not change gate priorities, budgets or the prediction-settling machinery — the value of the settlement record is that it stays comparable across runs. This adds a channel, not a rule. A forced call that then fails is still a failure and must count as one.
acceptance_criteria: A gate whose prediction names a tool forces that tool's fence on the following turn, and the met/unmet rate for those gates is measurable against gen-19's baseline.
notes:
BLOCKER FOUND WHILE BUILDING THE PLUMBING — do not close vf-00b assuming the wiring alone is enough.

DeepSeek serves prefix completion only from its BETA base URL, https://api.deepseek.com/beta. The running config uses https://api.deepseek.com/v1 (verified against /health). On /v1 the flagged trailing assistant message is not honoured, and the failure is silent: the request succeeds and the model answers after the message rather than continuing it, which looks exactly like an ordinary turn. So wiring the gates to prefill without also moving the base URL would produce no effect and no error, and would read as 'prefill does not help'.

Two consequences for this issue: (1) it needs a config change alongside the code, and the change affects every call the run makes, not just prefilled ones — worth confirming the beta endpoint behaves identically for ordinary completions before switching a campaign onto it; (2) it needs a positive check that the prefill actually took, otherwise there is no way to tell a working prefill from an ignored one. The cheapest check is that the response does NOT begin with the opener — a continued prefill starts mid-fence, an ignored one starts with prose or a fresh fence.

vf-614 and vf-24a are done and deployed; both are inert until something passes :prefill.
close_reason:
Implemented, tested and verified end-to-end against the live API.

Gates that predict exactly one tool (branch-out, repopulate — both 'the branch calls branch_theses') carry :tool; arbiter/decide passes it through and arbiter/prefill-for turns it into '```tool-call\n{"name": "branch_theses"'. Gates naming a choice (milestone: review-or-done) or a behaviour (stuck) get the bare fence, which still forecloses prose without the harness picking for the branch. Scoped to gated turns only — prefilling makes the response BEGIN with the call, which is right when already steering and wrong as a blanket default.

CORRECTION to what I filed here. I wrote that /v1 would ignore the prefix silently. It does not: DeepSeek rejects the request outright with 'prefix is only available when using beta api'. Safer, but it means a wrong base URL would fail EVERY steered turn, so supports-prefill? now takes config and checks for /beta — a /v1 config simply does not prefill and behaves exactly as today. Default base-url moved to /beta after verifying it serves ordinary completions identically.

Two bugs caught while wiring it, both of which would have been silent: the assistant message and journal assistant_text stored only the completion, leaving turns beginning mid-fence in the transcript and misrepresenting the format back to the model (fence/reattach now rebuilds the whole turn in both places); and truncated-without-call? re-parsed without the prefill, so a prefilled turn that HAD issued a call would have been billed a retry.

Live check: prefill '{"name": "branch_theses"' returned '}' and parsed as branch_theses with no parse error. 259 tests, 1290 assertions, 0 failures.

title: Every steering conclusion is n=1; there is no way to A/B a prompt or gate change
description:
Every conclusion drawn about steering is single-arm observation on one run each, and several are being acted on:

- vf-9sa: gen-19 gate predictions settled 4 met to 22 unmet, with milestone and tier-escalation both 0-for-4.
- vf-lho: gen-19 produced 32 artifacts and every one was fast-tier.
- gen-20 produced a slow-tier artifact at round 8 after its problem statement named verify_template and proof_step explicitly — which looks like evidence that naming tools works, but is one run, on a different problem, with different branches. An obvious confound.

None of these is measured. There is no way to run the same scenario twice under different prompts or gate settings and compare. prompt-digest (loop.clj:64) already fingerprints the system prompt plus gate config plus judge exemptions per run, which is exactly the arm identity such a comparison needs — and nothing consumes it.

WHAT TO MEASURE IS NOT THE MEAN. veriframe's interesting effects have the shape of blow-ups stopping, not typical runs improving: branches culled for nothing (vf-jki lost 2 of 5), gates firing without effect, a run that never touches the slow tier. Gating a comparison on the control arm's own spread would make exactly those effects invisible, because the spread is what the change removes. Report blow-up COUNTS and max-min dispersion alongside any mean, and let the dispersion thresholds be coarser than the mean ones, since range at small n claims less.

COST IS THE OBSTACLE. A campaign generation is hours of provider spend, so several runs per arm is not affordable at that scale. A cheap scenario — small fixed problem with a known answer, low max_turns, narrow beam — makes arms affordable without touching campaign runs, and is the thing to build first.
design: Three separable pieces, smallest first: (1) capture the cache token fields the provider already returns — adapter/openai.clj currently keeps only prompt/completion/total, so nothing can answer whether a wide beam thrashes the prefix cache; (2) a cheap fixed scenario with a known answer, runnable in minutes; (3) comparison reporting keyed by prompt-digest, on dispersion and blow-up counts as well as means.
acceptance_criteria: Two arms of the same cheap scenario can be run and compared on dispersion and blow-up count, with the arm identified by prompt-digest.
notes:
FIRST REAL COST DATA, from vf-4ef's usage capture, on gen-20's first 7 turns after resume (9 active branches):

  prompt 81,999  completion 20,949  cache hits 34,944  misses 47,055  ->  42.6% hit rate

Only 3 distinct cache_hit_tokens values across all branches, and most branches showed exactly 4,864 — the shared system-prompt prefix. Everything past it is a miss because each branch carries its own diverging transcript.

So the beam's caching story is: one shared ~4.9k prefix hits for every branch, and each branch's own history (3.5k-8.7k and growing) misses every single turn. Per-branch prompt cost grows monotonically with its transcript and none of that growth is ever cached. At width 9 that is 47k wasted prompt tokens per round and rising.

This is the number that was unknowable before and it bears directly on vf-mm0's finding that beam_width is a floor: the cost of running wide is worse than branch-count alone suggests, because the uncached fraction grows per branch per turn.

Worth measuring over a longer window before drawing conclusions — 7 turns at one moment in one run. But it is the first time the question can be asked at all.

title: Nothing watches the model's output text for repetition
description:
veriframe records tool-call MECHANICS per turn — parse errors, repair count, fence count, truncation (llm/fence.clj, state/record-mechanics) — but nothing looks at the model's prose. No signal compares this turn's assistant text to the previous turn's, and nothing compares output against the system prompt.

The gap matters because the failure it would catch is one veriframe demonstrably has. A model that starts re-emitting the same block of reasoning produces turn after turn with no usable tool call, which is exactly the __no_call__ pattern that culled two branches in gen-20 (vf-jki). Today that surfaces only as a mechanics count with no indication of the cause: a model that rambled, one that emitted the wrong fence, and one that is looping all look identical in the record.

MEASURE BEFORE BUILDING. turns.assistant_text is already journalled for every turn, so the detector can be scored against gen-17, gen-18, gen-19 and gen-20 for zero provider spend. The honest first step is a backtest reporting how often a near-duplicate response precedes a __no_call__ turn or a cull. If the rate is low, this issue closes with a measurement and no code — which is the right outcome and much cheaper than building the guard first.

Distinct from vf-jki, which fixed what happens after a no-call turn. This is about seeing the cause.
design:
If the measurement justifies a detector, the natural home is fence/signals, which already returns per-turn mechanics and is already folded in by record-mechanics.

Two design points worth stating up front. First, similarity alone is not a loop: legitimate work repeats itself, a branch retrying a Lean proof will produce near-identical text on purpose. A usable detector needs repetition AND regularity — several near-matches at consistent spacing — or it will fire on honest retries. Second, the standing rule for mechanics signals holds: they may tune repair budgets and must never relax a verification gate, since a signal must not loosen the guard that fires on the thing it measures.
acceptance_criteria: A measured near-duplicate rate across the four completed runs, and a detector only if that measurement supports one.
notes:
BACKTEST RESULT (vf-a8h). 18 runs, 3,464 consecutive turn pairs, Jaccard over 5-gram shingles of assistant_text.

PROSE REPETITION ESSENTIALLY DOES NOT HAPPEN HERE.

  similarity distribution:  p50 0.008   p75 0.018   p90 0.050   p95 0.096   p99 0.258   max 0.694
  pairs >= 0.85: 0        pairs >= 0.7: 0        pairs >= 0.5: 13 (0.38%)

The metric is not broken — median similarity is 0.008, i.e. consecutive responses share almost nothing, and the single most similar pair in the entire corpus is 0.694. There is no threshold at which a near-duplicate detector fires on real data. A SimHash loop detector would be dead code.

Why, most likely: the harness appends a tool result and a fresh context block before every turn, so the model never sees the same prompt twice and never writes the same response twice. The failure mode this issue was filed against — a model re-emitting a prose block until the token cap — is one veriframe's own turn structure prevents.

AT THE TAIL THERE IS SIGNAL, AND IT IS TOO SMALL TO USE. Of the 13 pairs above 0.5, nine preceded a failure or no-call and six of those were __no_call__. But 13 pairs is 0.38% of the corpus: a perfect detector on them would catch 6 of 182 no-call turns, about 3%. And the threshold would have to sit near 0.5, where two texts are still substantially different — maximum tuning sensitivity for minimum payoff.

THE STRUCTURED SIGNAL IS ~10x BIGGER. Identical (tool_name, result) against the previous turn fires on 53 of 182 no-call turns (29.1%) and 38 of 1,189 failures (3.2%), needs no threshold, and is an exact comparison over columns already journalled. That is vf-e7g, now implemented.

ONE HONEST CAVEAT on that comparison: the 0.0% STRUCT rate on healthy turns is close to tautological, not measured precision — the predicate requires the previous turn to be a failure with identical result text, and a successful turn's result text differs by construction. So STRUCT's value is coverage of the failing population, not a demonstrated false-positive rate.

Closing as measured-and-not-worth-building, which is the outcome the acceptance criterion explicitly allowed for.
close_reason: Measured rather than built. Prose repetition does not occur in this harness: 0 of 3,464 consecutive turn pairs exceed 0.7 Jaccard, median 0.008, max 0.694. A detector would never fire. The real repetition is structured — identical (tool, error) on 29% of no-call turns — and is handled by vf-e7g. Numbers recorded in the notes.

title: gen-20: settle Q-1, poly-time stage 3 over an exponential stage-2 set
description:
Run 36bf3163-f789-4a1d-bf30-7f46402491a9, started 2026-08-13, beam width 5, max_turns 400, seeded from gen-19 (cd58e618).

The question (vf-izq): give a poly-time algorithm returning the flow the three-stage rule selects on an ARBITRARY instance — no unique-stage-2 assumption, so it must perform stage 3 over a set that can have 2^m elements — or prove no such algorithm exists under a standard complexity assumption.

DELIBERATE EXPERIMENT: the formulation names NO attack. gen-19's Q-2 prompt named the proof strategy outright ('exhibit an instance whose symmetry group acts transitively on its stage-2 optimal set') and that is exactly what shipped, so that run showed the harness executes a handed-over attack well but said nothing about whether it finds one. gen-19's prompt also named greedy edge-by-edge fixing as 'the obvious attack'; that is omitted here on purpose. Verified absent from the problem text before launch.

Also carries an explicit evidence standard: the load-bearing claim must be confirmed by verify_template or a closed proof_start/proof_step, not verify_smt/verify_lean/verify_octave alone. That is a live test of vf-lho — whether naming the slow-tier tools by name gets them used.
acceptance_criteria: Q-1 settled either way with its assumptions named, or an honest 'not settled, here is the obstruction' that does not restate the given facts as a result.
notes:
COMPLETED 2026-08-13. B3 shipped; 197 turns, 11 confirmed artifacts, ALL slow-tier; 7 abandoned, 3 culled.

THE ANSWER: 'STATUS: NOT SETTLED.' It settled neither the algorithm nor hardness, shipped three machine-checked abstract lemmas, and named exactly what would be needed to close the gap.

I VERIFIED all three independently — analytically and by 80,000 randomised trials, 0 counterexamples:
 (1) scalarization: Q<=Qmax, range(L)<=Lrange, K>Lrange, H>K*Qmax+Lrange => minimizers of H*C+K*Q+L are lex-min on (C,Q,L). Integrality gives delta <= -H + K*Qmax + Lrange < 0 on the C layer.
 (2) one-coordinate: coords in [-D,D], B=2D+1 exceeds the max swing 2D, so k_j+B*F is F-minimal then k_j-minimal.
 (3) greedy: prefix-minimality forces a_i < y_i at the first differing coordinate, so a is lex-least.

THE PREDICTION HELD, AND ON THE HONEST SIDE. My round-13 note said the obstruction was not coefficient bit-length but D itself — that the separable-convex-to-linear flow reduction is polynomial only if D is polynomial in ENCODING size, and that a branch could pass its own scalarization lemma while smuggling that in via 'poly-time flow solving is standard background', which is how gen-18's answer shipped a restriction it never priced. The shipped answer names precisely that: '(a) ... |k_e| <= D for an explicitly computed D ... (b) ... separable convex integer flow problem solvable in polynomial time ... the coordinate bound is a nontrivial flow-specific fact that I did not verify.' It refused rather than smuggled. done() was accepted first try, with no refusals — the answer was already scoped correctly when offered.

RUN QUALITY, best of the four generations:
 - 11/11 confirmed artifacts slow-tier, against gen-19's 0 of 16. The formulation-level evidence standard held for a whole run.
 - unfaithful 2 of 13 (15%), against gen-19's 14 of 32 (44%).
 - turns: 105 neutral, 57 failure, 21 mechanics, 14 success.
 - cost, on the 33 turns recorded after vf-4ef landed: 441,516 prompt + 185,752 completion tokens, 80.5% cache hit. Much better than the 42.6% measured mid-run — the beam had collapsed to fewer branches by then, which is itself the vf-mm0 cost story in miniature.

Q-1 REMAINS OPEN. vf-izq stays open. The three lemmas are the lexicographic core any future algorithm or hardness proof would need, so a gen-21 has a real foundation rather than a restatement.
close_reason: Run completed and verified. Q-1 not settled; three lemmas confirmed independently. vf-izq stays open.

title: Nudge gates fire, settle unmet, and change nothing: 4 met to 22 unmet in gen-19
description:
gen-19 (cd58e618) fired 35 gates. Of the 26 whose predictions settled: 4 met, 22 unmet — a 15% hit rate. By gate:

  milestone          0 met / 4 unmet
  tier-escalation    0 met / 4 unmet   (see vf-lho)
  branch-out         2 met / 7 unmet   (+1 unsettled)
  repopulate         1 met / 4 unmet
  emergency-review   1 met / 2 unmet
  progress-stalled   0 met / 2 unmet   (+3 unsettled)
  stuck              0 met / 3 unmet   (+5 unsettled)

The prediction machinery itself is working — the gates settle honestly, which is how this is even measurable, and that is the design paying off. What the numbers say is that FIRING a gate does not reliably change what a branch does next. Every milestone prediction ('the branch calls review or done within two turns') went unmet.

Contrast with the gates that refuse rather than nudge: the audit gate rejected 14 of 32 artifacts in the same run, and those refusals demonstrably redirected work (B4 needed three encodings, turns 22/24/26, before the automorphism argument was accepted). Refusal works. Suggestion does not.

Worth measuring across gen-17/18 before acting — this may be a long-standing property that only became visible once predictions were settled.
design: The asymmetry suggests the lever is control, not phrasing: a gate that withholds something (an artifact, a done(), a branch slot) gets acted on; a gate that appends a message to the transcript competes with everything else in the context. Candidate: convert the worst offenders (milestone, tier-escalation) from message-appending to precondition-enforcing.
acceptance_criteria: Either the nudge gates' met-rate rises materially, or the ineffective ones are removed so they stop consuming budget and reading as supervision.
notes: Re-measured across gen-22/23/24 (2026-08-15): progress-stalled 12 met / 25 unmet, stuck 5/10, tier-escalation 2/4, safe-state 0/2. safe-state turned out to be a different bug entirely — missing from arbiter/settle's dispatch, so unmeetable; fixed in vf-9bo. The rest stand, but a high met-rate may only mean the gate predicted what the branch would have done anyway, so do not act on these until vf-fq6 gives a way to A/B.

title: tier-escalation never lands: a whole run confirmed on the fast tier only
description:
gen-19 (cd58e618) produced 32 artifacts and every one is tier=fast. No artifact in the run went through the harness's own heavy-verification paths: every SMT artifact used plain z3_check (tools.clj:592) rather than the dual-encoding cross-checked path (tools.clj:645), and all 9 Lean artifacts came from one-shot lean_check (tools.clj:1563) rather than interactive tactic mode closing a goal (tools.clj:1650).

The tier-escalation gate exists precisely to catch this — gates.clj:270, predicate (not (contains? (:tiers-seen branch) :slow)) — and it fired 4 times. All 4 predictions ('the branch runs a slow-tier check') settled UNMET.

Consequence is not cosmetic: the run's shipped headline result (no symmetry-invariant tie-break exists) rests on artifacts the harness only ever fast-checked. The 'confirmed by Z3 and independently by Octave' in the answer is the model choosing to run two tools, not the harness's dual-encoding check. The vocabulary implies a stronger guarantee than was obtained.

A gate that fires, burns budget, and changes nothing is worse than no gate — it makes tiers-seen look supervised when it is not.
design:
CORRECTION to the original design note. done() does NOT lack a cross-check rung — tools.clj:1366 already refuses when there is neither a passing review nor a slow-tier verify_template artifact ('Nothing has been independently cross-checked'). So the requirement I proposed partly exists.

The real finding is narrower and more interesting: the rung offers TWO routes and the review route is always taken while the verify_template route never is. gen-19's B4 shipped via review — the 'passing cross-review' in the answer text — which is a model-directed differently-shaped encoding judged by a reviewer, not the harness's built-in dual encoding. That is a real check, just a weaker one, and the answer's vocabulary does not distinguish them.

Revised options: (1) make the two routes distinguishable in the shipped record, so a reader can tell a reviewed claim from a template-cross-checked one; (2) have tier-escalation name verify_template and proof_start/proof_step explicitly rather than describing 'a slow-tier check', which is not a callable name; (3) require the template route specifically for claims the thesis marks as load-bearing, leaving review sufficient elsewhere.

Slow-tier producers, for reference: verify_template (tools.clj:645) and proof_step closing a goal (tools.clj:1650). Everything else — verify_smt, verify_lean, verify_octave, verify — is fast.
acceptance_criteria: A run that ships a done() answer has at least one slow-tier artifact behind the shipped claim, or the refusal says why not.

title: The nREPL listen socket is inherited by every engine subprocess
description:
Twin of vf-k0a, on the socket that fix did not cover. lsof against the live server:

  jolt   46865  10u  127.0.0.1:7888 (LISTEN)
  swipl  47093  10u  127.0.0.1:7888 (LISTEN)
  swipl  47095  10u  127.0.0.1:7888 (LISTEN)
  swipl  47097  10u  127.0.0.1:7888 (LISTEN)
  swipl  47099  10u  127.0.0.1:7888 (LISTEN)

Four swipl, one per branch in gen-19's beam, all holding the nREPL listener on fd 10. Port 3985 was clean, because vf-k0a's fix covers the vendored ring adapter only — this socket is created by jolt.nrepl in jolt core, with the same raw FFI socket/bind/listen and no close-on-exec.

Consequence is the same and it bites the workflow this project depends on: the port stays bound while any engine subprocess lives, so killing the server leaves the next start unable to bind its nREPL — which is the one channel for patching a live run without restarting it.

FIXED in jolt, branch fix/nrepl-socket-cloexec (58e0cc8b), pushed and awaiting a PR: SOCK_CLOEXEC on Linux, fcntl F_SETFD elsewhere on POSIX (bound with :varargs, since a fixed-arity fcntl corrupts the stack-passed argument on Apple arm64), and neither on Windows, which uses HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT. Verified by spawning a sleep beside a live nREPL and listing the port's holders: only the jolt process, where the same probe previously showed the child too. jolt unit suite clean.

NOT yet in effect here: veriframe runs the installed jolt 0.7.6, which predates this. The running server still shows the four swipl.
acceptance_criteria: lsof on a running veriframe server with a warm beam shows only jolt holding the nREPL port.
close_reason: Fixed in jolt 0.7.9 (7bf6c497 + CI test b9c4753e). Verified on the live server: lake/repl forked with both listeners open and inherited neither; only jolt holds 7888 fd 9 and 3985 fd 4.

title: gen-17 and gen-18 have no write-up
description:
The prior generation produced docs/phase-unwrapping.md. gen-17 (0d0c3560, 523 turns, 97 artifacts, 56 confirmed, 10 branches shipped) and gen-18 (65d50333, 603 turns, died ~20h in) have had none, so the three-stage canonical rule and everything gen-18 established about it exist only in the journal and in this session's notes.

Should cover at least:
- gen-17's headline: B4.2.2.3.2.2's three-stage rule (L1 -> Q=sum k^2 -> lex), proven well-defined in Lean. Stage 2 works because a Q level set lies inside a sphere in Z^E and is finite, collapsing the unbounded L1 argmin. The argument holds for real nonnegative weights, which is stronger than the natural-valued Lean version.
- gen-18's partial results on Q-A/Q-B/Q-C/Q-D, including that B2's poly-time algorithm covers only instances with a unique stage-2 minimizer and that this excludes the tied-path mechanism (vf-izq).
- The 12-vertex/16-vertex misdescription in gen-17's B4 (vf-6ai), which has no code fix and belongs here.
- What each shipped answer does NOT establish, since several ship explicit partial-result disclaimers.
close_reason: docs/phase-unwrapping-2.md covers both runs: the three-stage rule and why stage 2 is load-bearing, gen-18's Q-A/Q-B/Q-C/Q-D results with their restrictions, the vf-izq gap (poly-time algorithm excludes the tied-path mechanism), and vf-6ai (12-vertex graph described as 16-vertex, passed by both gates). 3x3 funnel independently re-derived over the cycle space.

title: close() did not release the listen port on Linux
description:
Found because the FD_CLOEXEC guard (vf-k0a) asserted the flag separately from its consequence. On CI the flag WAS set and the port still could not be rebound, which ruled out fd inheritance and pointed at shutdown.

stop-server set running? false and called close() on the listen fd. close() does not reliably wake a thread already blocked in accept(): macOS wakes it, Linux does not, so the accept thread kept the socket alive and the port stayed bound after stop-server returned. Next bind got address-in-use — the same symptom vf-k0a described, from an unrelated cause, which is exactly why the single-assertion version of that test was unreadable when it failed.

The adapter's own comment asserted the macOS behaviour as general: 'stop-server closes the listen fd (which unblocks accept)'.

FIXED: shutdown(fd, SHUT_RDWR) before close(). ENOTCONN from a listening socket on macOS is expected and ignored. Covered by the rebind half of server_test/a-subprocess-does-not-inherit-the-listen-socket; CI green on all four jobs including the Lean suite.
close_reason: Fixed by shutdown() before close() in vendor/ring_chez/adapter.clj; CI green on all four jobs.

title: Lean subprocesses inherit the server's listening socket
description:
lsof against a running jolt serve shows the HTTP listening socket held by three processes, on the same fd and the same kernel object:

  jolt  97090  4u  IPv4 0xb9638a5d078eee09  TCP 127.0.0.1:3985 (LISTEN)
  lake  97125  4u  IPv4 0xb9638a5d078eee09  TCP 127.0.0.1:3985 (LISTEN)
  repl  97149  4u  IPv4 0xb9638a5d078eee09  TCP 127.0.0.1:3985 (LISTEN)

lake/repl are the Lean pool's children (engine/lean-repl spawns lake env <repl-bin>). They inherited fd 4 because it is not marked close-on-exec.

Why it matters: the port stays bound as long as ANY holder is alive. Kill the server while a Lean session lingers — which is exactly what happens when a run is abandoned, since the repl is a long-lived process spawned with p/destroy-tree as a shutdown hook rather than a guarantee — and a restart fails with address-in-use against a server that is no longer running. The listener is also reachable by a subprocess that has no business holding it.

Applies to every subprocess the harness spawns, not just Lean: prolog and octave take the same path.

Fix is either O_CLOEXEC on the listening socket where it is created, or an explicit close in the child between fork and exec. Which one depends on what jolt.process exposes.
close_reason: Fixed in vendor/ring_chez/adapter.clj: close-on-exec! marks the listen fd and every accepted connection with FD_CLOEXEC via a :varargs fcntl binding (SOCK_CLOEXEC is Linux-only). Covered by server_test/a-subprocess-does-not-inherit-the-listen-socket, which spawns a child, stops the server and rebinds — red before (bind() failed on port 39187), green after. Verified live: lsof on a running server now shows only jolt on 3985, with the Lean repl warm and Mathlib imported.

title: The gl-area pointer goes stale while the widget is being replaced
description:
CORRECTED 2026-08-12 after looking at the full log rather than its tail.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS. glpane caches the widget as a raw pointer in st (:area, written only by on-realize). When the widget is destroyed and rebuilt, every request-render! between the destroy and the new on-realize hits freed memory, and GTK answers:

  Gtk-CRITICAL gtk_gl_area_queue_render: assertion 'GTK_IS_GL_AREA (area)' failed

Timestamps from one session — 15 criticals, not a steady stream:
  23:21:45 .. 23:22:13   13 of them, ~2.4s apart (the poll interval)
  (nothing for ten minutes)
  23:32:16, 23:32:25     2 more, exactly when start-run probes added runs

So it is a TRANSIENT window during widget replacement, and the pane RECOVERS when the replacement realizes. My original filing said the pane 'never repaints again' — that was wrong, inferred from a tail that happened to catch the burst. Severity is log noise plus a few dropped repaints, not a dead pane.

WHAT WAS FIXED. root renders a tree with no :gl-area in it while :composing? is true, so opening the new-run form genuinely destroys the pane. glpane/unmount! now clears the cached pointer and the GL object names, and toggle-compose! calls it on the way in; closing the form mounts a fresh area whose on-realize repopulates them. The misleading comment in root claiming the pane 'keeps its context' while the form is open is corrected.

WHAT IS NOT FIXED — the path that produced the criticals above. Neither burst came from the compose toggle: the first is at startup and the second coincides with runs appearing in the list. Both are re-render churn — root derefs @state and rebuilds the whole tree, and the :gl-area child is evidently being replaced rather than preserved, despite graph-pane being deref-free for exactly that reason. The real fix is either stable reconciliation for that child (a glimmer concern) or not caching a raw widget pointer across renders at all. Needs someone who can watch the window while toggling and selecting.

NOT COVERED BY A TEST. glpane requires glimmer-gl.gtk, so the headless suite cannot load it; nothing in test/ references glpane. The unmount! change is verified by reading, not by execution.
acceptance_criteria: No GTK_IS_GL_AREA assertion in the GUI log during a normal session, and the pane visibly repaints after a run is selected and after the poll loop updates.
notes: 2026-08-12 second pass. Compose-toggle destroy path fixed (glpane/unmount!). The observed bursts are NOT from that path, so the bug stays open — but realize! now detects and prints when it is handed a different area than the one cached, which is exactly the widget-replacement event. Next GUI session that produces the GTK critical will also produce a line naming it, turning an inferred cause into a recorded one.
close_reason:
Fixed at the mechanism rather than by enumerating the ways a widget can die. glpane now connects to the gl-area's own GTK 'unrealize' signal via glimmer.ffi/g-signal-connect-data and clears the cached pointer and GL objects when it fires; realize! puts them back. That covers every teardown — the new-run form (which renders a tree with no :gl-area), glimmer's positional reconciler destroying a child when a slot's tag changes, and reparenting — without needing a hook glimmer does not have. The callable is retained, since a collected one leaves GTK holding a dangling function pointer, and each widget is wired once.

Verified: handler id came back 404 (nonzero — an invalid signal name returns 0 and warns), no gsignal warning, and a 60s GUI session against a live run produced an entirely empty log where the same window previously produced a 13-critical burst. The replacement-detection println is kept as a backstop, since the only evidence this bug ever gave was a GTK critical with nothing naming the transition.

title: A Lean import line cost 19 turns across two runs
description:
Snippets are elaborated against a session that already has Mathlib, so an import inside one is illegal. Lean reports only: invalid 'import' command, it must be used in the beginning of the file. True, unactionable, identical every time, and the model retries.

Counted across the two phase-unwrapping runs: 19 turns. gen-18 alone hit it on 7 branches (B2, B2.3.3, B2.3.3.3 x2, B3 x2, B4.3 x5, B4.3.3 x2, B4.3.3.2). B3 spent two of the six failures that culled it on this, while pursuing the convex-cost-flow reduction.

strip-lean-imports now drops import lines in lean-repl/run-command, which covers every caller. open lines are left alone since they are legal against an existing env, and a line merely mentioning the word is untouched.
acceptance_criteria: A snippet with a leading import runs instead of erroring; open lines and identifiers containing 'import' survive.
close_reason: strip-lean-imports added, tested, deployed into run 65d50333 over nREPL.

title: B2's Q-A class excludes the tied-path mechanism, and the answer does not say so
description:
gen-18 B2 (run 65d50333, T62) settled Q-A for instances with a UNIQUE stage-2 minimizer. The algorithm and correctness proof are right — I verified the scalarization, the [-D,D] bound, and the outside-the-box argument independently.

But the restriction excludes the tied-path mechanism entirely:
  3x3 grid, 9 L1-minimizers, Q = [6,6,6,6,6,6,8,8,10] — six tie at the minimum
  one dipole gadget, 2 minimizers, both Q=2
  m gadgets, 2^m minimizers, all Q=2m
  5-vertex zero-weight cycle — stage-2 minimizer IS unique, so this one is covered

Stage 2 collapses infinite ambiguity and does nothing about combinatorial ambiguity. The open part of Q-A is therefore exactly stage 3: lexicographic selection over a Q-tied set.

The answer states the restriction in its first sentence but never says which established instances fall outside it, and every reader of this campaign would want that.
acceptance_criteria: The write-up states which of the campaign's own instances are outside B2's class, and gen-19's formulation targets stage 3 over a Q-tied set as the remaining open part of Q-A.
notes: gen-19 (cd58e618) was pointed at this as Q-1 and did NOT settle it. It answered Q-2 instead (no symmetry-invariant tie-break exists, proven on the two-path dipole square) and measured Q-3 on 3x3. The greedy attack named in the prompt — fix k(e_1) to its least stage-2-optimal value, then k(e_2), ... — was not settled either way. Still the open question: lexicographic least over a 2^m stage-2 set without enumerating it. See docs/phase-unwrapping-2.md gen-19 section.

title: Clean turns did not work off the cull budget
description:
consecutive-failures was cleared only by :success, which in practice means banking an artifact. A branch that hit a rough patch and then worked productively still carried the stale count into the cull gate.

gen-18 B1 made three malformed tool calls, then three clean Octave runs producing dual potentials, and was culled on a counter last incremented three turns before. The guard against well-formed but useless calls is turns-since-progress, which a neutral turn still increments, so decaying the failure count on a clean turn gives nothing away.
acceptance_criteria: A neutral turn decrements consecutive-failures, floored at zero; sustained failure still outpaces recovery.
close_reason: Fixed, tested, deployed into run 65d50333 over nREPL.

title: Repopulation is an invitation with no prediction, declined 9 times in 12
description:
Run 0d0c3560, first 120 turns: 12 repopulate invitations, 3 accepted. Every acceptance came when the beam was already collapsing (B4 declined twice at alive=3 and accepted at alive=1). The current phase is 5 consecutive declines at alive=3, one every turn or two, rotating across branches because the cooldown is per-branch.

Two problems, neither of them 'repopulation does not work' — it does, and all four of this run's forks came from it.

First, it is an invitation, not a gate. It appends a message directly in the scheduler instead of going through the arbiter, so it carries no prediction, settles nothing, and appears in no gate tally. The decline rate was invisible until someone counted branch-opened events by hand. This is the exact reasoning that turned branch-out from an invitation into a gate: 'an invitation the model may decline is not a mechanism; a gate with a settled prediction is.' Repopulation was left behind.

Second, being outside the arbiter it is a second harness voice on the same boundary as whatever gate fired, so 'at most one steer per boundary' holds for gates only.

Fix: make it a gate. The precondition needs facts only the scheduler has (alive count, target, which branch is strongest), so the scheduler should mark the chosen branch and the gate should read the mark.
acceptance_criteria: A repopulation ask is recorded as a gate firing with a prediction, settles met or unmet like every other gate, and cannot land on the same boundary as another steer.
close_reason: Repopulation is now the :repopulate gate (priority 6, above branch-out): the scheduler marks the strongest survivor and the gate does the asking, so it carries a prediction, settles met/unmet on branch_theses, appears in the gate tally, and cannot land on a boundary that already had a steer. Budget :max-repopulates. Covered by agent_test/repopulation-is-a-gate-with-a-prediction-not-an-invitation.

title: Enumerate and close the finite sub-257 four-prime supports
description:
Finding 11 (gen-15) proved every density-feasible four-prime support outside the three dense base triples {3,5,7}, {3,5,11}, {3,5,13} has all primes < 257, and the bound is sharp ({3,5,17,251} is feasible at 2.000156). That list is finite and has never been enumerated, let alone closed.

Enumerate them explicitly, then close each with the per-class LP at whichever Q divides the support. With the sibling families this completes the four-prime tier.
acceptance_criteria: The finite list is enumerated with a stated count, and each member is closed or explicitly left open with a reason.

title: Close the two remaining four-prime families with the per-class LP
description:
Finding 12 closed {3,5,7,11} and with it all {3,5,7,q}, using the per-class assignment LP instead of the M_g bound. The same method is UNTRIED on the two sibling families.

By monotonicity in the fourth prime, each family reduces to its smallest member:
- {3,5,11,q} -> {3,5,7,11} at Q=165. Old M_g bound there: -2303/480.
- {3,5,13,q} -> {3,5,7,13} at Q=195. Old M_g bound there: -1729/576.

Both are exactly the situation at Q=105, where M_g gave -647/480 and the LP was infeasible for all 9,835 orbits. Method: fix the unit-weight residues (WLOG the prime ones to 0 by translation), derive F1 and A_g from P, build the LP with y_{g,b} >= 0, sum_b y_{g,b} <= A_g, every uncovered class needing 1-F1, and sweep orbits under multiplication by units mod Q (order phi(165)=80, phi(195)=96).

Closing both, plus the finite list below, gives 'every odd covering system needs at least five distinct odd primes'.
acceptance_criteria: The per-class LP is checked over all orbit representatives at Q=165 and Q=195, with the orbit count stated and the constants derived from P.

title: Retry a __no_call__ turn with a doubled budget
description:
A branch that spends its whole output budget reasoning and never emits a tool call is a process failure, not evidence - the same thing vf-mti fixed for the judge, on the branch loop instead. Currently the turn is scored a failure, the harness appends 'Think less and call a tool', and the branch loses the turn.

Seen on gen-11 (90336412) turn 1: all three branches produced 48-51k characters, hit the 16384 cap, and called nothing. It self-corrects once conversation history exists (turn 3 was down to 4.7k), so the cost is a first-turn tax that scales with how dense the seeded brief is - and the brief gets denser every generation.

Fix: on __no_call__, retry once inside the same turn with a doubled max-tokens, journalled like judge-retry. Reuse the arithmetic-heavy sizing from tools/judge-max-tokens so a brief full of exact rationals opens high instead of paying for the doomed call first.

title: Start a new run from the GUI

title: Size the judge's token budget to the claim, not retry into it
description:
Measured on gen-10 (05ecb88a): audit/review are the beam's critical path. In rounds of width>=7 they were the straggler 24 of 28 times while taking ~24% of turns; verify_lean gated a round once in 47 turns and verify_smt never. 39 of the run's 46 judge-retries land after turn 40, when claims became exact-rational assertions over 20-26 moduli. The judge burns its output budget re-checking the arithmetic, hits the cap with no verdict, and is retried at doubled max-tokens - so an arithmetic-heavy audit costs 2-3 calls.

Fix: estimate the needed budget up front (claim length, count of rational literals / large denominators) and open the audit at the higher cap when it looks arithmetic-heavy, keeping retry as the fallback rather than the norm. Should cut the tail that sets round wall-clock while the other branches sit at the advance-all barrier.

title: beam_width is a floor, not a cap: a run can grow to 15 concurrent branches
description:
gen-20 was started with beam_width 5 and was running 9 active branches (11 total) at round 26.

This is by design and the code says so. repopulate only fires when alive < target (beam.clj:245), so width is a floor it refills toward; growth above it comes from the branch-out gate, bounded by :max-total-branches, whose value is 15 and whose doc calls it a cost ceiling: 'every branch is a concurrent provider call per turn plus its own engine process.'

The gap is between that and what the API name implies. POST /v1/runs takes beam_width, the runs row stores beam_width, and a caller setting 5 reasonably expects at most 5 concurrent provider calls per turn. The actual ceiling is 3x that, and the cost is real: at 9 active branches the run was carrying 9 concurrent provider calls per round, and seven Lean REPLs were alive at the time.

Not filed as a bug because the behaviour is deliberate and documented in gates.edn. Filed because the naming hides a 3x spend multiplier from whoever sets the parameter.
design: Cheapest honest fix is documentation plus reporting: say in the API docs that beam_width is the repopulation target and max_total_branches is the ceiling, and report both on the run detail endpoint so a running beam's actual width is visible. A stricter option is to scale max-total-branches from the requested width rather than fixing it at 15, so asking for a narrow beam actually gets one.
acceptance_criteria: Someone setting beam_width can predict the maximum concurrent branch count, and the run's actual width is visible while it runs.
close_reason: Implemented and tested. Usage capture turned out bigger than filed: the adapter parsed usage and client/chat returned it, but the agent loop dropped it and turns had no columns, so the harness could not report what a run cost at all. Migration v4 adds prompt/completion/total plus the cache split, nullable so a provider-error turn does not claim to be free.

title: /health reports the configured share-artifacts?, not the value a seeded run actually uses

beam.clj:671 forces :share-artifacts? true for any run started with a seed-run, overriding config. /health reports the config value, so during gen-20 it said share-artifacts? false while the run had sharing on and had fired 91 shared-artifact-hit events.

Found while trying to explain those 91 events against a health endpoint that said sharing was off. Cost a detour; a run-level setting reported as a global one is the kind of thing that makes a later investigation start from a false premise.
design: Either report the effective per-run value on the run detail endpoint, or have /health say that the config value is a default a seeded run overrides. The run row already records enough to derive it.
acceptance_criteria: Nothing reports a sharing state that contradicts the run's behaviour.
